In 1812 one man ruled or controlled almost everything on this map between Lisbon and Warsaw. Within three years he was on a rock in the South Atlantic.

Europe at Napoleon's peak — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Start with the dark blue. The French Empire on this map is not France. It has swallowed Belgium, the Netherlands, the German North Sea coast as far as Hamburg, Catalonia, and a strip of the Adriatic called the Illyrian Provinces.

2/ Those coastal annexations weren't hunger for land. They were customs enforcement. Britain couldn't be invaded, so Napoleon tried to bankrupt it by closing the continent to British trade — and smuggling ports had to be governed directly to be closed.

3/ Now the satellites. The Confederation of the Rhine replaced a Holy Roman Empire of some 300 statelets that Napoleon dissolved in 1806. The Duchy of Warsaw was Polish in everything but the name — he never let them call it Poland.

4/ Spain looks split because it was. The Peninsular War had been grinding since 1808: a French king in Madrid, a Spanish resistance in the hills, and a British army under Wellington working up from Portugal. Napoleon called it his ulcer.

5/ Look at Sweden, in blue-grey and not in the French camp. Its crown prince was Jean Bernadotte — a French marshal, elected to the Swedish succession in 1810. In 1812 he sided with Russia against the country he was born in.

6/ Two quiet lines on the map mattered enormously. Ottoman Wallachia and Moldavia: in May 1812 the Sultan made peace with Russia at Bucharest, releasing a Russian army from the south — weeks before Napoleon crossed the Niemen in June.

7/ He went in with the largest army Europe had ever assembled, on the order of half a million men. A fraction came back. The map you're looking at is the high-water mark, and it was already draining when it was drawn.
